title: ExxonMobil (XOM) Stock: Surge as Pioneer Launches $2.1 Billion Senior Notes Tender - Blockonomi
content: ExxonMobil (XOM) stock rose 1.00% to $161.07 on Tuesday after recovering from an intraday low near $159.00. The gain came as subsidiary Pioneer Natural Resources launched tender offers covering $2.1 billion of outstanding senior notes. The transaction gives Pioneer a route to repurchase debt due in 2030 and 2031. Pioneer Natural Resources offered to purchase all outstanding notes across two separate senior debt series. The offer covers $1.1 billion of 1.900% senior notes scheduled to mature in 2030. It also includes $1 billion of 2.150% senior notes due in 2031. ExxonMobil owns Pioneer following its major acquisition of the shale producer, which expanded its Permian Basin operations. Therefore, the tender process forms part of financial activity within ExxonMobil’s broader corporate structure. Pioneer will cancel any notes that it successfully purchases through the offers. The company placed no minimum principal requirement on either tender offer. Therefore, the transactions can proceed regardless of the total amount submitted by eligible noteholders. However, Pioneer must still satisfy or waive applicable conditions outlined within the formal offer documents. Pioneer will calculate the payment for accepted notes using Treasury yields and predetermined fixed spreads. The 2030 notes carry a fixed spread of 30 basis points over the reference Treasury security. Meanwhile, the 2031 notes carry a 35-basis-point spread over the same reference security. Both series use the 4.375% United States Treasury security due August 31, 2031, as their pricing benchmark. Pioneer will determine the applicable reference yield using the bid-side yield reported through Bloomberg. The resulting repurchase yield will combine that Treasury yield with each series’ fixed spread. Holders will also receive accrued and unpaid interest for notes accepted under the tender process. Pioneer will calculate that interest through the settlement date, excluding the settlement date itself. Interest will then stop accruing once the company completes payment for accepted notes. Both tender offers will expire at 5:00 p.m. New York City time on September 14, 2026. Pioneer may extend or terminate the offers earlier if the transaction conditions allow such action. Holders must submit valid tender instructions before the stated expiration deadline. The company expects to determine final pricing at 2:00 p.m. New York City time on September 14. Pioneer expects settlement to occur on September 16, two business days after the scheduled expiration date. However, any extension of the offer could also shift the settlement schedule. Holders may withdraw submitted notes before the expiration deadline under the tender terms. After that deadline, submitted tenders generally become irrevocable unless applicable law provides additional withdrawal rights.  shares are back in focus this week as crude benchmarks firm on the back of escalating tensions between the United States and Iran, with the Strait of Hormuz emerging once again as a flashpoint for global energy markets. The Irving, Texas-based energy major finds itself at the center of renewed attention as traders and physical buyers alike weigh how a prolonged standoff around one of the world's busiest maritime chokepoints could complicate tanker movements and reshape near-term supply flows. Global benchmark crude has firmed steadily in recent sessions as the standoff between the United States and Iran shows little sign of a near-term resolution. Strikes and counter-strikes attributed to both sides have kept shipping insurers and tanker operators on alert, with several carriers reportedly rerouting or pausing transits through the Strait of Hormuz altogether. Because the strait remains one of the few chokepoints through which such a large share of the world's crude and liquefied natural gas must pass, even a partial disruption tends to ripple quickly through global benchmarks. Energy watchers note that the current episode differs from past flare-ups in that it has persisted for an extended stretch rather than fading within a trading session or two, keeping a structural premium embedded in prices. For integrated energy companies such as ExxonMobil, a firmer crude complex tends to support upstream cash generation even as it raises input costs for downstream and chemical operations elsewhere in the portfolio, a dual exposure that helps explain why integrated majors are often viewed differently from pure upstream producers whenever Middle East tensions dominate headlines. ExxonMobil ranks among the largest publicly traded energy companies, with operations spanning upstream production, refining, chemicals and a growing low-carbon solutions unit. The company's upstream base includes production in the Permian Basin, offshore Guyana, and a series of international joint ventures spanning Africa, the Middle East and Asia-Pacific. Its downstream network includes some of the largest refining complexes in North America, while its chemicals arm has increasingly become a focal point for capital allocation as the company looks to capture margin in higher-value polymer and specialty product lines. The company's scale gives it a degree of flexibility that smaller independent producers do not enjoy, allowing capital to move across geographies and business lines depending on where the strongest economics present themselves at a given point in the cycle. That flexibility has become especially relevant as commodity swings tied to Middle East supply concerns complicate planning across the wider sector. Among the corporate developments drawing attention alongside the broader crude move is ExxonMobil's continued build-out of chemical capacity along the Gulf Coast. The company has been advancing a blending and processing expansion tied to its Proxxima line of resin technology, a project aimed at supporting higher-margin applications in construction, wind energy components and other specialty end markets. The expansion reflects a broader shift within the major oil companies toward diversifying revenue away from pure commodity crude and gas sales and toward differentiated chemical products that carry less direct exposure to swings tied to geopolitical supply scares such as the current Iran-related standoff. Company disclosures have described the Gulf Coast chemicals push as part of a multi-year plan to widen margins across the downstream and chemical segments, a plan that continues even as attention elsewhere in the market remains fixed on the crude price reaction to Middle East developments. Separately, ExxonMobil continues to advance a deepwater program off the coast of Nigeria, an area where the company has held long-standing acreage and infrastructure. Progress on a large-scale deepwater development in the region, alongside continued spending on an adjacent field already in production, underscores the company's willingness to commit capital to long-cycle upstream projects even during a period of elevated volatility tied to Middle East tensions elsewhere in the world. Nigeria's deepwater basins have drawn renewed attention from several international majors in recent years as easier onshore acreage has become harder to access amid community and regulatory friction. ExxonMobil's continued build-out in the region signals confidence in longer-dated production economics even as near-term headlines remain dominated by the Iran-U.S. standoff and its implications for the Strait of Hormuz. ExxonMobil's upstream growth engine continues to rely heavily on two flagship positions: the Permian Basin in West Texas and New Mexico, and its offshore acreage in Guyana. Both areas have delivered steady production increases in recent years, supported by continued development drilling in the Permian and phased expansion of floating production vessels offshore Guyana. Neither program is directly tied to the Middle East, but both benefit from the same firmer crude backdrop that has accompanied the current Iran-U.S. standoff, since higher realized prices on barrels produced from these assets flow straight through to segment cash generation. Company disclosures have continued to point to further phases of Guyana development moving through planning and permitting stages, pointing toward continued expansion of the region as a core growth pillar regardless of how the near-term Middle East situation resolves. Across the wider energy complex, companies with exposure to Middle East production or shipping routes have been reassessing near-term planning in light of the Hormuz-related disruption. Some tanker operators have added war-related surcharges to freight rates, while several buyers of Middle East crude grades have reportedly sought alternative cargoes from West Africa, the U.S. Gulf Coast and other Atlantic Basin sources to reduce reliance on shipments that must transit the strait. For ExxonMobil, the practical effect of the standoff has been an incremental increase in global benchmark pricing, which flows through to realized prices on the company's own production regardless of where that production is physically located. While upstream production tends to benefit from a firmer crude tape, ExxonMobil's downstream refining network faces a more mixed picture. Higher crude feedstock costs can compress refining margins unless product prices keep pace, and the company's refineries along the Gulf Coast and elsewhere have had to navigate that balance closely during the current period of elevated crude pricing. Historically, ExxonMobil's refining segment has demonstrated resilience during geopolitical supply scares by adjusting crude slates and maximizing higher-value product yields, a flexibility that partly explains why integrated majors tend to weather crude spikes somewhat more evenly than refining-only operators. Fuel marketing operations across the company's branded retail network add a further layer of diversification, since retail fuel pricing tends to adjust with a lag relative to wholesale crude moves, offering a partial buffer during periods of rapid benchmark price swings tied to episodes such as the current Strait of Hormuz standoff. Beyond its traditional hydrocarbon business, ExxonMobil has continued to build out a low-carbon solutions unit focused on carbon capture, hydrogen and related technologies, positioning the company to participate in the broader energy transition alongside its core oil and gas operations. While this unit remains a small part of the overall business relative to upstream and downstream operations, its continued build-out reflects a broader industry pattern among integrated majors of hedging longer-term strategic exposure across both traditional and emerging energy technologies. The unit's progress has continued largely independent of near-term crude price swings tied to episodes such as the current Strait of Hormuz tensions, reflecting its longer development horizon relative to core production and refining operations. Company commentary has framed the low-carbon push as complementary to, rather than a replacement for, the core hydrocarbon business, with cash generated from upstream and downstream operations continuing to fund the bulk of near-term capital spending across the broader portfolio. Beyond the immediate Iran-related headlines, the broader oil and gas sector continues to navigate a set of structural trends, including a slower pace of new large-scale discoveries, continued consolidation among mid-sized producers, and growing emphasis on capital discipline relative to the aggressive expansion cycles seen in prior decades. Companies across the space have generally prioritized steady production growth, disciplined spending and consistent payouts to holders over rapid output expansion, a stance that has left the sector somewhat better positioned to absorb short, sharp demand or supply shocks such as the current Hormuz-related episode. ExxonMobil's positioning as a fully integrated major, spanning upstream, downstream, chemicals and an emerging low-carbon unit, continues to differentiate it from pure-play exploration and production companies that carry more concentrated exposure to crude price swings. That diversification has historically supported steadier cash generation across commodity cycles, even if it means the company captures a smaller proportional benefit during sharp upside crude moves compared with upstream-focused peers. Alongside the Gulf Coast and Nigeria projects, ExxonMobil recently confirmed its routine quarterly distribution to holders of record, a step that continues a long-running pattern of consistent payouts regardless of near-term commodity swings. The company has also continued to discuss capital commitments tied to its broader upstream portfolio, including ongoing work in the Permian Basin and offshore Guyana, both of which remain central to production growth plans over the coming years. Management commentary in recent public disclosures has pointed to continued emphasis on cost control across the upstream and downstream segments, alongside steady progress on the chemicals expansion program. The company has signaled that capital spending will remain broadly disciplined even as crude firms, reflecting a wider industry preference for steady, predictable spending programs over reactive increases tied to short-term price swings. Despite the near-term crude tailwind tied to Middle East tensions, integrated majors continue to navigate a set of longer-running challenges, including the need to balance traditional hydrocarbon production with growing pressure to diversify into lower-carbon energy sources, rising costs tied to complex deepwater and unconventional projects, and the logistical complexity of operating across dozens of countries with differing regulatory regimes. The current Hormuz-related episode adds a layer of near-term uncertainty on top of those structural challenges, particularly for companies with production or shipping exposure closer to the Middle East. ExxonMobil continues to compete with a small group of similarly scaled integrated majors, alongside a broader set of independent upstream producers with more concentrated exposure to specific basins such as the Permian or the Bakken. The current environment of firmer crude tends to narrow the performance gap between integrated majors and pure upstream producers, since both groups benefit from higher realized prices on production, even as the majors' downstream and chemical segments introduce a partially offsetting dynamic. The renewed focus on Middle East supply routes has broader implications beyond individual companies, feeding into a wider category of coverage tracked across the S&P 500, where energy sector weightings can shift meaningfully during periods of sustained crude strength. ExxonMobil, as one of the largest constituents within that index's energy sector grouping, tends to see its own share price movements watched closely as a proxy for broader sentiment toward the group whenever geopolitical supply concerns dominate headlines. As the standoff between the United States and Iran continues to unfold, market participants are likely to keep a close watch on developments around the Strait of Hormuz, given the outsized role that waterway plays in global energy logistics. For ExxonMobil specifically, the interplay between firmer crude, ongoing Gulf Coast chemical expansion and continued deepwater development off Nigeria positions the company as a useful bellwether for how integrated majors are navigating the current period of heightened geopolitical uncertainty. Broader interest in the space, including coverage tracked under Oil and Gas Stocks, continues to reflect how supply-side jitters in the Middle East ripple through integrated majors, independent producers and service companies alike. title: ExxonMobil Has Raised Its Dividend 43 Years Running. Here's the One Year the Streak Almost Broke. - The Motley Fool
content: ExxonMobil is one of the most reliable dividend growers in the U.S., but that dependability was threatened in a big way in 2020. Lengthy dividend increase streaks are appealing to income investors, but it pays to remember that streaks reflect something that's already occurred. They're not future projections. Even some companies that were once Dividend Kings, or those firms with payout increases in at least 50 consecutive years, have turned into dividend offenders. As one example, 3M cut its payout in 2024, ending a 64-year streak. ExxonMobil nearly became a dividend offender in 2020. Image source: Getty Images. One way of interpreting the end of a long run of boosted dividends is that no company is immune from joining that dubious club. ExxonMobil (XOM +0.75%) nearly gained entry into that infamous group in 2020, threatening what was, at the time, a dividend-increase streak spanning more than three decades. Since 2020 was the year in which the oil giant's dividend was most recently vulnerable to negative action, the obvious culprit was the COVID-19 pandemic. Due to significant demand destruction, there was a brief period in 2020 when U.S. oil prices were negative, prompting doom-and-gloom scenarios for oil majors and their dividend-enthused shareholders. To its credit, Exxon averted dividend disaster at a time when some of its rivals did not. Both BP and Shell were among oil majors that cut payouts, citing the pandemic. For Shell, it was the first time the company had trimmed its dividend since World War II. In 2020, Exxon CEO Darren Woods acknowledged that the payout is "sacrosanct," pledging to emphasize a "reliable dividend" policy as the company worked through the effects of the global health crisis. Those efforts have paid, well, dividends because Exxon's payout increase now spans 43 years, and the company has adopted a policy of modest, though steady, annual increases that can keep the streak alive without straining the balance sheet. For the energy sector history buffs out there, Exxon does have a strike on its dividend record. In the first quarter of 1975, the company delivered a payout of $0.30 below the prior quarter, amid the global energy crisis. Todd Shriber has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. title: ExxonMobil's CEO Called Venezuela 'Uninvestable.' Trump Says It's Going In Anyway. Here's Why Investors Should Pay Attention. - The Motley Fool
content: Chevron's recently expanded agreement in Venezuela could provide a blueprint for Exxon's return. This past January, ExxonMobil's (XOM +0.75%) CEO Darren Woods called Venezuela "uninvestable" during a meeting at the White House, a remark that didn't sit well with President Trump. Fast forward a few months, and the President recently publicly announced that "Exxon is going in" to Venezuela. While ExxonMobil hasn't confirmed plans to reenter the country following its exit two decades ago, much has changed since the year began. Here's why investors should pay attention to the President's assertion that ExxonMobil is returning to Venezuela. At a recent press event unveiling a massive U.S. oil deal with Venezuela, President Trump highlighted that Exxon and Chevron (CVX +0.57%) are among the many big oil companies heading into Venezuela. Chevron has already confirmed its expansion in the country, noting that its two decades of patience have finally paid off. The oil giant recently announced that it has expanded its position in the country, as one of its joint ventures has been assigned rights to develop two adjacent oil fields. That supports Chevron's plans to invest more than $7 billion over the next five years to more than double its production in the country to around 600,000 barrels per day. The oil giant noted in the press release announcing its expanded position that the agreements include "enhanced fiscal, commercial, and legal terms intended to support durable and competitive long-term investments." That's something ExxonMobil investors should pay close attention to, because the company has previously said it needs durable investment protections and improved economics before it would commit to returning to Venezuela. The improved terms of Chevron's deal suggest that Venezuela appears willing to make the concessions that Exxon has been seeking as a condition of its return. While Trump's statement and Chevron's sweetened deal terms don't necessarily mean Exxon will return, they certainly hint at that to investors who are paying attention. title: Chevron Stayed in Venezuela for 20 Years While Rivals Left. Here's Why Its CEO Says Patience Pays Off. - The Globe and Mail
content: Chevron has maintained operations in Venezuela for over 100 years. Its decision to remain after ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips left has proven to be a major competitive advantage. Chevron's new agreement with Venezuela will enhance its resource position and the terms of its deal. Chevron(NYSE:CVX) just signed a landmark deal to significantly expand its operations in Venezuela. The agreement, which positions the oil giant to double its output over the next five years, is a testament to its patience. "You have to hang in there until all the conditions come together: the technology, the economics, the markets, the politics," stated CEO Mike Wirth in a recent interview with Bloomberg. It stayed long after rivals ExxonMobil(NYSE:XOM) and ConocoPhillips(NYSE:COP) left, putting it in a position to capitalize on this major opportunity to help revitalize Venezuela's oil industry. Here's a look at how Chevron's patience has proven to be a significant competitive advantage in Venezuela. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips both left Venezuela in 2007 after the country nationalized their assets. Both have been seeking restitution, with ConocoPhillips winning an arbitration award of $12 billion that it has been trying to recover for years. The oil companies have been considering a return this year, as they each sent technical teams to evaluate potential investment opportunities. While ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods called Venezuela "uninvestable" this past January, President Trump recently said that Exxon would be going back into Venezuela. However, both companies are far behind Chevron, which has maintained operations in the country for over 100 years. That's part of the company's patient strategy in the country. CEO Mike Wirth told Bloomberg: "You have to have some patience and look at this out over time and not become discouraged. Not pick up and leave when things are difficult." By hanging on during the tough times, which included dealing with hyperinflation, power outages, and unstable civil conditions, Chevron was able to pounce when the opportunity came around to participate in the revival of Venezuela's oil industry. Chevron has already been expanding its operations in Venezuela. In April, it consolidated its heavy-oil position in the country through an asset swap with Venezuela's national oil company, Petroleos de Venezuela, S. A. (PDVSA). It received an additional 13.21% working interest in Petroindependencia, increasing its stake in that joint venture (JV) to 49%. Additionally, its Petropiar JV (30% interest) was granted rights to develop the adjacent Ayacucho 8 area in the Orinoco Oil Belt. In exchange, Chevron gave up its interest in two gas licenses and in another non-operated joint venture. This trade enhances Chevron's ability to increase production by 50% by the end of 2028, from its recent rate of 280,000 barrels per day. Now, Chevron is further building on this legacy position with additional enhancements to its JVs. Its new deal with Venezuela will provide it with more acreage in the Orinoco Belt. Petroindependencia received the rights to develop the adjacent Carabobo-1 and Carabobo-2-South-A areas. Additionally, the deal includes enhanced fiscal, commercial, and legal terms that will support durable, competitive long-term investments in the country. Improved financial terms are something ExxonMobil has been seeking before it would agree to reenter the country. This increased position and improved terms support Chevron's new plan to invest more than $7 billion over the next five years. That would enable the company to more than double its production to around 600,000 barrels per day. Chevron estimates that its costs will be less than $20 a barrel, positioning it to drive strong earnings growth over the next five years from this investment. However, while Wirth told Bloomberg that it has "good, high-quality resource positions" in Venezuela, "They're also sometimes not the easiest resource to produce." That's a risk investors should keep an eye on as the oil company ramps up its investment rate in the country. There's also the potential for renewed political risks, both in Venezuela and from future elections in the U.S. Chevron's decision to remain in Venezuela during the tough times is paying off. Its existing joint ventures in the country are receiving additional resources, which, together with improved terms, will enable the company to significantly increase production over the next five years. Given its low-cost resources, it could generate meaningful cash flow growth. It now has a huge head start over Exxon and ConocoPhillips, both of which are still evaluating whether to reenter the country. That could benefit the oil stock in the long run, as its low-cost growth in Venezuela could give it the fuel to deliver higher total returns than its rivals over the next few years. Advisory Solutions Group LLC purchased a new stake in  ExxonMobil Corporation (NYSE:XOM - Free Report) in the second quarter, according to the company in its most recent filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The fund purchased 7,864 shares of the oil and gas company's stock, valued at approximately $1,075,000. Several other institutional investors have also recently made changes to their positions in XOM. Berbice Capital Management LLC purchased a new position in  ExxonMobil in the fourth quarter valued at about $26,000.  E Fund Management Hong Kong Co. Ltd. increased its position in  ExxonMobil by 456.1% during the 4th quarter. E Fund Management Hong Kong Co. Ltd. now owns 228 shares of the oil and gas company's stock valued at $27,000 after buying an additional 187 shares in the last quarter.  Aventus Investment Advisors Inc. acquired a new position in  ExxonMobil during the 2nd quarter valued at about $27,000.  Keewaydin Investments LLC purchased a new stake in  ExxonMobil in the fourth quarter valued at about $33,000.  Finally, Portus Wealth Advisors LLC purchased a new stake in  ExxonMobil in the first quarter valued at about $36,000. Hedge funds and other institutional investors own  61.80% of the company's stock. NYSE:XOM opened at $159.53 on Friday. The company has a 50 day moving average price of $152.97 and a 200-day moving average price of $152.25. The company has a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.12, a current ratio of 1.13 and a quick ratio of 0.85. ExxonMobil Corporation has a 1-year low of $108.35 and a 1-year high of $176.41. The firm has a market cap of $661.24 billion, a price-to-earnings ratio of 20.53, a price-to-earnings-growth ratio of 0.98 and a beta of 0.18. ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM - Get Free Report) last announced its quarterly earnings results on Friday, July 31st. The oil and gas company reported $3.52 earnings per share for the quarter, missing the consensus estimate of $3.56 by ($0.04). The business had revenue of $114.53 billion during the quarter, compared to analysts' expectations of $109.94 billion. ExxonMobil had a net margin of 8.88% and a return on equity of 13.14%. During the same quarter in the prior year, the firm earned $1.64 EPS.  Equities research analysts forecast that  ExxonMobil Corporation will post 11.98 EPS for the current year. The business also recently disclosed a quarterly dividend, which will be paid on Thursday, September 10th. Shareholders of record on Monday, August 17th will be issued a dividend of $1.03 per share. This represents a $4.12 annualized dividend and a yield of 2.6%. The ex-dividend date of this dividend is Monday, August 17th. ExxonMobil's dividend payout ratio (DPR) is presently 53.02%. Here are the key news stories impacting ExxonMobil this week: XOM has been the topic of a number of research analyst reports. Wall Street Zen upgraded ExxonMobil to a "hold" rating in a research note on Saturday. Citigroup  reiterated a "neutral" rating on shares of ExxonMobil in a research note on Wednesday, July 8th. Bank of America lowered ExxonMobil from a "buy" rating to a "neutral" rating and increased their price objective for the company from $154.00 to $158.00 in a report on Tuesday, July 28th. Piper Sandler raised their price objective on ExxonMobil from $158.00 to $185.00 and gave the stock a "neutral" rating in a research note on Thursday. Finally, HSBC  set a $158.00 price target on shares of ExxonMobil in a report on Monday, August 3rd. Ten research analysts have rated the stock with a Buy rating and twelve have given a Hold rating to the company's stock. According to data from MarketBeat.com, ExxonMobil  has an average rating of "Hold" and a consensus price target of $167.45. ExxonMobil Corporation NYSE: XOM is an integrated oil and gas company engaged in the exploration, production, refining, distribution and marketing of petroleum products and the manufacture and sale of petrochemicals. Its operations span the full energy value chain, including upstream exploration and development of crude oil and natural gas; midstream transportation and storage; and downstream refining, product distribution and retail. The company also produces a broad range of chemical products for industrial and consumer applications. ExxonMobil markets fuels and lubricants under well-known brands such as Exxon, Mobil and Esso, and its Mobil 1 motor oil is a prominent consumer product.
